title: The ranks
hookLine: by those ranged in ranks, the angels, and the believers in rows for prayer (37:1)

cards: Watch the start of a Friday prayer in a big mosque, from the balcony if you can. Hundreds of people are milling around, finding spots, greeting friends. Then the call to stand comes.
People step forward, shoulder to shoulder, heel to heel. Gaps close. Lines straighten.

In a few seconds, a crowd becomes rows, as straight as if someone had drawn them with a ruler. Surah thirty-seven opens with an oath on exactly that kind of line, though the first ones it means aren't on earth.

teach.b: The surah is called As-Saffat. Its first verse is an oath: wa's-saffati saffa, by those ranged in ranks. The root, s-f-f, means a row, a line.
Many commentators say these are angels, standing in rows before their Lord, waiting for His command.

Near the end of the same surah, in verses commentators read as the angels speaking, they describe themselves that way: we are those who stand in ranks, and we are those who glorify. So the first rows aren't human at all.
Then the hadith brings the picture down to earth. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ asks his companions: won't you line up the way the angels line up before their Lord? They ask how the angels line up.
He says: they complete the front rows first, and they stand close together.
Another hadith, in both Bukhari and Muslim, says: straighten your rows, for straightening the rows is part of establishing and completing the prayer.
So the row isn't only tidiness; many Muslims understand it as copying the angels. And it does something. In a row, the rich man and the driver stand shoulder to shoulder.

teach.h: A ROW WITH NO RESERVED SEATS.
teach.b: Nobody has a reserved seat. Whoever arrives first fills the front. The line itself teaches something about equality before Allah, without anyone having to say it.

how: Before congregational prayer, the imam often tells the people to straighten their rows; worshippers stand shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot, filling the front rows first.

o: the levels of paradise, one above another
rows of angels before their Lord, in As-Saffat
soldiers lined up for battle in early Islam

p: the root: a row, a line

s: many commentators say the ranks in 37:1 are angels
angels standing in rows before their Lord; they describe themselves so near the surah's end.
in the mosque, important people have reserved places in the front rows
whoever arrives first fills the front; the row has no reserved seats.
straightening the rows is only about neatness
a hadith calls it part of completing the prayer, and another links it to how angels line up.

games.q: the Prophet asks his companions: won't you line up the way the angels line up before their Lord? they ask how. what's his answer?
o: they complete the front rows first and stand close.
games.why: they complete the front rows first and stand close together, a hadith in Sahih Muslim.

practice: Sit or stand tall, feet even, shoulders level, as if you were in a row with someone on either side. If something near you is crooked, books on a shelf, shoes by the door, straighten one line of them, slowly, with care.
Then return to stillness and picture the rows: angels before their Lord, and people shoulder to shoulder below.

wordCard.voice: The ranks. As-Saffat, the rows: angels standing before their Lord, and believers who straighten their lines for prayer to stand the way the angels stand. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: by those ranged in ranks, the oath that opens surah thirty-seven.

carryVoice: Your line: in ranks. The first rows were in heaven, and the mosque floor copies them. Until tomorrow.
